**Ruby version**: ruby 3.4.5 (2025-07-16 revision 20cda200d3) +PRISM [x86_64-linux]


### Other notes

This issue was not recognized before because in well-orchestrated systems the opportunity window for this race condition is minimal, so I understand this would probably not be high on the community's priority list to fix. 
In our case it has a big impact, because we also implemented an auto-save feature for that model (the changes are saved as the user types), and this feature is like saving and opening the form very quickly—resulting in conflicts (with oneself) every time. 

I mostly wish to communicate the issue and seek guidance. Solutions I considered: 

#### 1. `has_rich_text: ..., analyze_blobs_async: false` 

For the price of performance, avoid race conditions completely

#### 2. Disable bubbling up the touch events somewhere along the chain.

This risk cache bugs, so no-go

#### 3. Once Removed Content Model and Main Model: 

Instead of `Note  has_rich_text:` make `Note has_one: :content` and `Content belongs_to: :note; has_rich_text: ` 
This has the same issue as 2 of breaking cache

#### 4. Implement custom ActionText::RichText and ActiveStorage::Blob implementations, and force sync blob analyze.

Essentially 1, but not on the framework level 

#### 5. Force save if the lock_version indicates a conflict, but the conflict is with oneself

Maybe possible for our specific setup.

comments.author: g-pavlik
comments.body: Update: After thinking about the problem for a while, I think there's no "framework level" solution for this issue, so I think we should at least document this edge case: #55799

comments.author: joshuay03
comments.body:
Thank you for the detailed report.

I'm wary of suggesting changes like this, but this might be a good opportunity to question whether `#analyze` should be touching the record at all—that is, whether it should use `#update!` or something like `#update_columns` instead: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/36da3909403a9ca9b5e9c4a2da9e89bef1500d85/activestorage/app/models/active_storage/blob/analyzable.rb#L30

My thinking is that this is enriching existing data rather than making a user-initiated change, and therefore shouldn't be running validations and callbacks. Active Record encryption behaves similarly, using `update_columns` to transform data representation without triggering validations or callbacks: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/36da3909403a9ca9b5e9c4a2da9e89bef1500d85/activerecord/lib/active_record/encryption/encryptable_record.rb#L190

Regarding this:
> 2. Disable bubbling up the touch events somewhere along the chain.
>
> This risk cache bugs, so no-go

I don't think this should be a concern because:
1. The blob was already attached – When the user uploads and saves the attachment, the parent record is already touched/saved, so the cache is already invalidated at that point. The subsequent analysis is just enriching metadata on a blob that's already associated.
2. Metadata is usually not semantically significant – Image dimensions, duration, etc. are typically used for display optimisation, not core content. If your view is already rendering the blob (which it can do before analysis completes), obtaining the dimensions shouldn't require re-rendering the parent.

Let's wait for the core team to weigh in. If this doesn't move forward, we can proceed with your documentation PR.

comments.author: joshuay03
comments.body: @g-pavlik Rather than wait for someone from Core/Committers to give the go-ahead, would you be interested in sending a PR for my proposed change first so we can gather feedback there? I'm happy to do so myself if not. If we don't get any feedback after a while, [we can share it in the Discord server](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#get-some-feedback) to try and get a review.

comments.author: g-pavlik
comments.body:
@joshuay03 Thanks a lot! I did some research, and touching the parent model was a part of an actual bug fix. So removing it seems like a no-go. 
I made a PR rails/rails#57284 that allows touching parent models without changing the lock_version column (more details there). I'd love to read what you think.

title: CONTENT_TYPE header is not cleared between ActionController::TestCase requests
need_summary: The developer asked if the persistent CONTENT_TYPE header between ActionController::TestCase requests poses a security risk and how to resolve it; the answer provides a concrete fix by resetting CONTENT_TYPE in the process_controller_response ensure block (see the provided code snippet and line reference).
security_topic: clearing CONTENT_TYPE header between test requests
question_text: Should the `scrub_env!` method be changed to also delete `CONTENT_TYPE` from the env?
answer_text: The fix follows your suggestion to reset `CONTENT_TYPE` in the `process_controller_response` method's ensure block (around line 664), alongside the existing cleanup for XHR headers and `query_string`.
thread_text:
ISSUE #55759: CONTENT_TYPE header is not cleared between ActionController::TestCase requests
Author: arielj
Date: 2025-09-24T20:38:34Z
Labels: stale
State: closed

[c0]
### Steps to reproduce

- Create an `ActionController::TestCase` test
- Perform a `get` request test after a `post` request test
- Notice the `get` requests has the wrong content type

Sample application https://github.com/arielj/content_type_is_not_cleared

Check https://github.com/arielj/content_type_is_not_cleared/commit/99eed7080c886d8cd421ba663362178bb60041f3 for the details.

- Clone the repo
- Run `rails test`
- Notice this is printed to the console:

```
GET request. Content type: 
POST request. Content type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
GET request. Content type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
```

### Expected behavior

The content type should be cleared for the get request

### Actual behavior

The content type is whatever was set by the previous non-get request.

This was not always creating issues for us, but with an update of the Rack gem and some changes in Rails 7.2 (producing `content_length == nil` instead of `content_length == 0`), if a POST request is done with multipart data and then, after that, a GET request is done, the incorrect content_type header makes Rack attempt to [parse a non-existent multipart content](https://github.com/rack/rack/blob/14c8731436785d7e79a4db0f3304769a26083182/lib/rack/request.rb#L513) during the GET request because `form_data?` is true, incorrectly.

My understanding is that the [`scrub_env!` method](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/2ef3103c8d79eae9ccb4ab32691fd072ea932537/actionpack/lib/action_controller/test_case.rb#L671-L672) should be changed to also delete `CONTENT_TYPE` from the env.

If anyone can confirm this I can make a PR changing this.

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.0.3 for the sample app, but we identified it at least since rails 6.1

**Ruby version**: 3.4.5 for the sample app, but we identified it at least since Ruby 3.1


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @Edouard-chin 2025-09-24T23:31:03Z:
Hello thanks for reporting the issue. As mentioned in the doc, you can only test a single controller action per test inside an action controller test case https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/lib/action_controller/test_case.rb#L250

If you need to test multiple endpoints inside a test, please use an [integration test](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/testing.html#integration-testing) instead.
---
[c2] @arielj 2025-09-25T12:31:34Z:
> Hello thanks for reporting the issue. As mentioned in the doc, you can only test a single controller action per test inside an action controller test case https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/lib/action_controller/test_case.rb#L250
> 
> If you need to test multiple endpoints inside a test, please use an [integration test](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/testing.html#integration-testing) instead.

just curious then, why do we have a `scrub_env!` method then that clears the request object before a request in the test?

because over time there were PRs merged fixing similar issues making more than one request in a single test like https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/32773 and https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/32673

In practice, it has always had code to handle multiple request in a single action controller test and even fixes were accepted for that AFTER that comment was already in place
---
[c3] @Edouard-chin 2025-09-25T12:37:50Z:
Ah, that's true, thanks. I wasn't aware we had fixed similar issues which now sets a precedence. I'll reopen and let the team decide whether this should be fixed. I also wonder if that comment about performing a single action is worth adding then?
---
[c4] @guilleiguaran 2025-10-15T06:14:20Z:
@arielj hey!! Please open a PR updating `scrub_env!` and reference this issue, or let me know, and I'll fix it.
---
[c5] @arielj 2025-10-16T19:55:47Z:
Hey @guilleiguaran we tried this change with @FionaDL and we ran into some issues that we are not sure how to handle.

The basic idea was to add `env.delete 'CONTENT_TYPE` to the [`scrub_env!`](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/lib/action_controller/test_case.rb#L671) method, but we noticed that is not going to work because it's common for people to set a request content type modifying the `@request.headers` object before the request, and it's done also in other tests like: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/test/controller/test_case_test.rb#L607.

We can't just delete this or the beginning of the test request will clear it at this line: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/lib/action_controller/test_case.rb#L526.

We then thought that we could clear the content type header AFTER the request is done, but there's also a common pattern to do assertions against the `@request` object after the request like in this test: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/test/controller/test_case_test.rb#L640.

So, we can't clear it before or after the request.

----

Maybe we have to handle this first with a deprecation warning to deprecate assigning the content_type header directly and encourage using the `:as` option in the request methods?

Since `:as` is processed after the new TestRequest is created, we could encourage that. It would allow people to set the content type they want for a given request but also allow us to clear the content type so it's not leaking to the next requests silently.

What do you think? Do you think it makes sense? Is it worth it?

Do you have any advice as to where the right place to add this deprecation warning would be? We were thinking that we can do something like this in: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/lib/action_controller/test_case.rb#L526C9-L526C106:

```
if !as && @request.content_type
  # show the deprecation warning here
  # this would mean the request is done with a content type header that was not set with the `:as` option
  # so it either came from a user setting `@request.headers["Content-Type']` or from the previous request
end
@request          = TestRequest.new scrub_env!(@request.env), @request.session, @controller.class
...
```

And eventually in another Rails version the `scrub_env!` method could actually be changed to delete the content type header.
---
[c6] @guilleiguaran 2025-10-24T05:10:03Z:
@arielj II had a chance to look at this a bit closer. Examining the code, it looks like using the `content_type=` setter (https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/lib/action_controller/test_case.rb#L84) is also a valid pattern:

```ruby
@request.content_type = "application/json"
get :action
```

and deleting the `CONTENT_TYPE` on the `scrub_env!` will get rid of the header in this case as well.

The good news is that `Content-Type` isn't the only header that needs to be cleaned after running the test; we also need to clean the XHR headers and reset the `query_string`, so resetting the content_type there might be a good idea:
https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/lib/action_controller/test_case.rb#L659-L663

I don't think we should guarantee that the headers remain unmodified after the request finishes, and that isn't the case for the XHR headers. For testing the headers' values during the request, as intended in https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/test/controller/test_case_test.rb#L637, I think we should update the tests to use the `test_headers` action defined, e.g:

```ruby
    post :test_headers, as: :json

    env = ::JSON.parse(@response.body)
    assert_equal "application/json", env["CONTENT_TYPE"]
```
---

[c8] @Saidbek 2026-01-22T09:21:52Z:
Hey @arielj and @guilleiguaran! 👋

I've looked into this issue and implemented a fix based on the discussion. I created an inline test script to reproduce the issue, which you can run to see the problem in action:

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails"
end

require "action_controller/railtie"
require "minitest/autorun"

class TestApp < Rails::Application
  config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f
  config.root = __dir__
  config.eager_load = false
  config.hosts << "example.org"
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"

  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)
end
Rails.application.initialize!

Rails.application.routes.draw do
  get "/", to: "test#index"
  post "/", to: "test#create"
  post "/test_headers", to: "test#test_headers"
end

class TestController < ActionController::Base
  include Rails.application.routes.url_helpers
  skip_before_action :verify_authenticity_token

  def index
    content_type = request.headers["CONTENT_TYPE"] || request.headers["Content-Type"] || "none"
    render plain: "GET request. Content type: #{content_type}"
  end

  def create
    content_type = request.headers["CONTENT_TYPE"] || request.headers["Content-Type"] || "none"
    render plain: "POST request. Content type: #{content_type}"
  end

  def test_headers
    render plain: ::JSON.dump(request.headers.env)
  end
end

class BugTest < ActionController::TestCase
  tests TestController

  def setup
    @routes = ActionDispatch::Routing::RouteSet.new
    ActionDispatch.deprecator.silence do
      @routes.draw do
        get ":controller(/:action)"
      end
    end
    super
  end

  def test_content_type_persists_between_requests
    get :index
    assert_response :success
    assert_nil @request.headers["CONTENT_TYPE"], "First GET should have no CONTENT_TYPE"

    post :test_headers, params: { foo: "bar" }
    assert_response :success
    env = ::JSON.parse(@response.body)
    assert_equal "application/x-www-form-urlencoded", env["CONTENT_TYPE"], "POST should set CONTENT_TYPE during request"

    assert_nil @request.headers["CONTENT_TYPE"], "CONTENT_TYPE should be cleared after POST completes. Got: #{@request.headers['CONTENT_TYPE'].inspect}"

    get :index
    assert_response :success

    content_type = @request.headers["CONTENT_TYPE"]
    assert_nil content_type, "CONTENT_TYPE should be cleared between requests. Got: #{content_type.inspect}"
  end
end
```

The fix follows your suggestion to reset `CONTENT_TYPE` in the `process_controller_response` method's ensure block (around line 664), alongside the existing cleanup for XHR headers and `query_string`. I've also updated the tests to check headers during requests using the `test_headers` action.

Would you mind taking a look when you have a chance? Happy to make any adjustments! 🙏

title: Production SSL not enforced by default
need_summary: The developer needed to know why setting both config.assume_ssl and config.force_ssl to true does not force HTTPS redirects, answered with an explanation that AssumeSSL middleware fakes HTTPS requests causing force_ssl to see the request as secure, citing the Rails middleware source code links as the anchor.
security_topic: force_ssl not redirecting when assume_ssl is enabled
question_text: Shouldn't `force_ssl` ensure that HTTP requests are redirected to HTTPS no matter the other configuration options are set? Enabling both `force_ssl` and `assume_ssl` still allows HTTP requests which doesn't seem right.
answer_text:
My understanding of `config.assume_ssl` is that you use it when you want your application to accept HTTP requests but behave as if receiving `https` requests. Basically, Rails "[fakes](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/lib/action_dispatch/middleware/assume_ssl.rb#L13-L25)" the request as if it is an `HTTPS` request if you turn `config.assume_ssl` on, so because of that, when the `config.force_ssl` part is triggered, it sees the request as an `HTTPS` request.

The official doc for this config says:

>  When proxying through a load balancer that terminates SSL, the forwarded
  request will appear as though it's HTTP instead of HTTPS to the application.
  This makes redirects and cookie security target HTTP instead of HTTPS. This
  middleware makes the server assume that the proxy already terminated SSL, and
  that the request really is HTTPS.

Here is how I came to this conclusion:

1. [Rails creates some middlewares by default](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/4e72506c57a9ad570136b0a169d1b1612d9f24b8/railties/lib/rails/application/default_middleware_stack.rb)
2. `assume_role` middleware goes first, and then `force_ssl` [(source)](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/4e72506c57a9ad570136b0a169d1b1612d9f24b8/railties/lib/rails/application/default_middleware_stack.rb#L20-L27)
3. When a request is received, the AssumeSSL middleware will force update some headers to tell Rails the request should be processed as an `HTTPS` request [(source)](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/lib/action_dispatch/middleware/assume_ssl.rb#L13-L25).
4. Then, the SSL middleware looks at the request to see whether or not it is an `HTTPS` request [(source)](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/lib/action_dispatch/middleware/ssl.rb#L88-L100).
5. The check for `request.ssl?` will return true as we are already faking the request to be an `HTTPS` request; therefore, no redirect to enforce SSL will be executed.

So maybe a better option would be to raise a warning to alert the user about `assume_ssl` behaviour when both configs are set to `true`.

Author: scottclk

Labels: pinned

### Steps to reproduce
SSL is not enforced by default as `config.assume_ssl` and `config.force_ssl` don't work when both set to `true`.

<!-- (Guidelines for creating a bug report are [available
here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#creating-a-bug-report)) -->

<!-- Paste your executable test case created from one of the scripts found [here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#create-an-executable-test-case) below: -->
```sh
# Create a new rails app
$ rails new ssl-check
$ rails g controller Static index

# Check default options
$ cat config/environments/production.rb | grep ssl
config.assume_ssl = true
config.force_ssl = true

# Build and run container
$ docker build -t ssl-check .
$ docker run -d -p 80:80 -e RAILS_MASTER_KEY=<master-key> --name ssl-check ssl-check
Rails 8.0.2.1 application starting in production

# HTTP Request
$ curl -I http://localhost/static/index
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```

### Expected behavior

- HTTP requests should force redirect to HTTPS unless: `config.force_ssl = false`


### Actual behavior

- HTTP requests are allowed when both `config.assume_ssl` and `config.force_ssl` are set to `true`
- HTTPS forced when `config.assume_ssl = false` and `config.force_ssl = true`

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.0.2.1

**Ruby version**:  3.4.5

need_summary: The developer asked why the `loader` attribute is no longer supported and how to configure ActiveStorage securely, answered by referencing the Rails commit 2d612735ac0d9712fdfffaf80afa627e7295f6ce and the `config.active_storage.supported_image_processing_methods` setting.
security_topic: configuring allowed image processing methods after security hardening
question_text: The TIFF conversion to PDF should continue to pass in Rails 8.0.2.1
answer_text:
https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/2d612735ac0d9712fdfffaf80afa627e7295f6ce#r164396337

> Feel free to modify the list in your application, this is just the default so that Rails is more secure by default.

> https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/dd96c7129be574e5a4edc491192f3cd68c1ab814/activestorage/lib/active_storage/engine.rb#L133-L134

> It appears to be missing from the Configuring guide (PR welcome if you want to add it)

> ```
> config.active_storage.supported_image_processing_methods = [ ]
> ```

ISSUE #55528: Breaking functionality after patch
Author: leom806
Date: 2025-08-21T19:54:25Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
### Steps to reproduce

You will also need a `config/storage` with a basic `test` service set up:

```yaml
test:
  service: Disk
  root: <%= Rails.root.join("storage") %>
```

And also a `spec/fixtures/sample.tiff` with any TIFF file:
[sample.tiff](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21925383/sample.tiff)

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails", "8.0.2.1" # ---> Tests passes with Rails 8.0.2

  gem "sqlite3"
  gem "image_processing"
end

require "active_record/railtie"
require "minitest/autorun"
require "active_storage/engine"

# This connection will do for database-independent bug reports.
ENV["DATABASE_URL"] = "sqlite3::memory:"

class TestApp < Rails::Application
  config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f
  config.eager_load = false
  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"

  config.active_record.encryption.primary_key = "primary_key"
  config.active_record.encryption.deterministic_key = "deterministic_key"
  config.active_record.encryption.key_derivation_salt = "key_derivation_salt"

  config.active_storage.service = :test
  config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick
end
Rails.application.initialize!

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :posts, force: true do |t|
  end

  create_table :active_storage_attachments do |t|
    t.string     :name, null: false
    t.references :record, null: false, polymorphic: true, index: false
    t.references :blob, null: false
    t.datetime   :created_at, null: false
    t.index      [:record_type, :record_id, :name, :blob_id], name: "index_active_storage_attachments_uniqueness", unique: true
  end

  create_table :active_storage_blobs do |t|
    t.string   :key,        null: false
    t.string   :filename,   null: false
    t.string   :content_type
    t.text     :service_name, null: false
    t.bigint   :byte_size, null: false
    t.string   :checksum, null: false
    t.datetime :created_at, null: false
  end

  create_table :active_storage_variant_records do |t|
    t.belongs_to :blob, null: false, index: false
    t.string :variation_digest, null: false
    t.index %i[ blob_id variation_digest ], name: "index_active_storage_variant_records_uniqueness", unique: true
    t.string :variation_key
  end
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_one_attached :file do |attachable|
    # [loader, saver, apply] were removed in Rails 8.0.2.1
    attachable.variant :tiff_to_pdf, convert: :pdf, format: :pdf, loader: { page: nil }
  end
end

class BugTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  def test_tiff_to_pdf_variant
    post = Post.create!
    post.file.attach(io: File.open(Rails.root.join('spec', 'fixtures', 'sample.tiff')), filename: 'sample.tiff', content_type: 'image/tiff')
    post.file.variant(:tiff_to_pdf).processed

    assert_equal 'application/pdf', post.file.variant(:tiff_to_pdf).image.blob.content_type
    assert_equal 'sample.pdf', post.file.variant(:tiff_to_pdf).image.blob.filename.to_s
  end
end
```

### Expected behavior

The TIFF conversion to PDF should continue to pass in Rails 8.0.2.1

### Actual behavior

It is failing because the `loader` attribute is no longer supported

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.0.2.1

**Ruby version**: ruby 3.2.2 (2023-03-30 revision e51014f9c0) [arm64-darwin22]

> https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/dd96c7129be574e5a4edc491192f3cd68c1ab814/activestorage/lib/active_storage/engine.rb#L133-L134

title: ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector sets cookies on asset requests
need_summary: The developer asked whether asset requests should set a session cookie, and the maintainer replied that it’s a bug in Propshaft, pointing to the Propshaft railtie file at commit e49a9de659ff27462015e54dd832e86e762a6ddc as evidence.
security_topic: asset requests setting cookies unexpectedly
question_text: it made me wonder if it's correct for asset requests to respond with a cookie.
answer_text:
This IMO is a bug in propshaft. It's mounted inside the Rails routes: https://github.com/rails/propshaft/blob/e49a9de659ff27462015e54dd832e86e762a6ddc/lib/propshaft/railtie.rb#L48-L50

So it's invoked after all rack middlewares.

Instead, it should probably be early in the rack middleware chain, likely right after `ActionDispatch::Static`.

Now the good news is that this is a development only setup (should be fixed regardless).

ISSUE #55508: ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector sets cookies on asset requests
Author: EmilioCristalli
Date: 2025-08-17T17:53:16Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
Not sure if this is a bug, but noticed that when using the automatic DB switching ([docs](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_multiple_databases.html#activating-automatic-role-switching)), with the default resolver `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver` and context `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver::Session`, it seems like requests for assets are getting a cookie sent back in the response.

Noticed this while investigating issues with system tests not rendering flash messages correctly, and it looks like it was happening because of race conditions between redirect requests and asset requests, causing it to override the cookie and remove the flash message. This might be a different issue on our side (that we are not properly waiting for asset requests to finish before submitting a form or something like that), but it made me wonder if it's correct for asset requests to respond with a cookie.

I don't know too much about the session and cookie management, but from what I could debug, it seems like this is happening because the `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver::Session` middleware reads `request.session[:last_write]`, so it's like it makes it load the session, and maybe this makes `ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore` send the cookie back in the response?

### Steps to reproduce
Created [this repo](https://github.com/EmilioCristalli/test_db_selector) to reproduce the issue. Has a few commits with the steps to create the app, but it's a normal Rails app with scaffold for one model (Post). 

The last commit in main has the automatic db switching enabled, but moving one commit back (to `9232d6768d`) should disable it to see the difference.

Can open the root page (which loads posts#index) and observe any asset requests (like http://localhost:3000/assets/application-bfcdf840.js) in the developer tools to see the `Set-Cookie` header in the response.

### Expected behavior
The asset requests shouldn't have a `set-cookie` header in the response.

(not 100% sure this is the expected behavior, but it looks like it's what happens when automatic DB switching is not enabled)

### Actual behavior
Asset requests have a `set-cookie` header in the response.

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.0.2.1
**Ruby version**: 3.4.5

ISSUE #55460: `Rails.logger` is not `#freeze`-friendly
Author: joshuay03
Date: 2025-08-07T05:15:42Z
Labels: activesupport
State: closed

[c0]
### Steps to reproduce

<!-- (Guidelines for creating a bug report are [available
here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#creating-a-bug-report)) -->

<!-- Paste your executable test case created from one of the scripts found [here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#create-an-executable-test-case) below: -->

Not exactly a bug, but more of a question about whether `Rails.logger` should be `#freeze`-friendly.

We're implementing a custom railtie that freezes `Rails.logger` to prevent unintentional modifications by gem initializers or application code. This addresses a recurring issue where we've accidentally changed the Rails logger level when configuring logging for gems that share the same logger instance.

For example, when a gem shares `Rails.logger` and we configure its logging level in an initializer like:
```ruby
# config/initializers/some_gem.rb

SomeGem.logger.level = Logger::DEBUG  # Oops! This changes Rails.logger.level too
```

This has happened a few times in our codebase, causing production log level changes that resulted in either lost log messages (when accidentally set to a higher level) or excessive logging (when set to a lower level).

The railtie works by freezing the logger after Rails completes its logger setup but before any `config/initializers` run. However, we discovered that Rails' `ActiveSupport::LoggerThreadSafeLevel` module attempts to modify the logger's singleton class when accessing `.level`, which fails when the logger is frozen (see link in code comment).

Our current workaround is to call `Rails.logger.level` before freezing to trigger the lazy initialization of the thread-local key, but this feels like an implementation detail we shouldn't have to know about. It would be ideal if Rails loggers were designed to be freeze-friendly, allowing safe freezing without requiring knowledge of internal lazy initialization patterns.

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

# This railtie freezes the singleton Rails logger instance to prevent unintentional modifications
# during initialisation or runtime. This ensures that in production, we don't lose log messages due
# to a config initializer for a gem changing the logger level when sharing the same logger instance.
#
class FreezeLoggerRailtie < Rails::Railtie
  # rspec-mocks relies on proxies for method stubbing and expectations,
  # and frozen objects cannot be proxied.
  unless Rails.env.test?
    initializer :freeze_logger, after: :initialize_logger, before: :load_config_initializers do
      # We need to read the logger level before freezing the logger because the thread-local key to store
      # the level is lazily assigned to an instance variable.
      #
      # See: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/3235827585d87661942c91bc81f64f56d710f0b2/activesupport/lib/active_support/logger_thread_safe_level.rb#L43-L45
      Rails.logger.level
      Rails.logger.freeze

      if Rails.logger.is_a?(ActiveSupport::BroadcastLogger)
        Rails.logger.broadcasts.each do |logger|
          logger.level
          logger.freeze
        end
      end
    end
  end
end

```

### Expected behavior

<!-- Tell us what should happen -->

Calling `Rails.logger.level` or `Rails.logger.info` or any common method on `Rails.logger` shouldn't raise an error when `Rails.logger.freeze` has been called beforehand.

### Actual behavior

title: Container fails to initiate when built with certain permissions
need_summary: The issue was whether the Dockerfile’s permission handling caused a security‑related container start failure, which was fixed in #54428 (see the updated Dockerfile at railties/lib/rails/generators/rails/app/templates/Dockerfile.tt#L115).
security_topic: container entrypoint permission denial due to file ownership
question_text: Container fails to initiate when built with certain permissions
answer_text: This is already fixed in #54428. The Docker user now owns all the files. ref: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/railties/lib/rails/generators/rails/app/templates/Dockerfile.tt#L115
thread_text:
ISSUE #55438: Container fails to initiate when built with certain permissions
Author: returnDanilo
Date: 2025-08-02T01:51:40Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
The Dockerfile provided by rails is configured to make the container initiate as a (hopefully) unprivileged user with UID 1000. By the way the Dockerfile is structured, it makes some files in the image end up owned by root, regardless what user owned it originally. While the "others" unix permission field inherits from the original file.
This makes it so that an image built from a project in which all files have permission 770 will fail to have a container launched from it, because the UID 1000 user can't access a root-owned 770 file.

This is a problem because users commonly restrict permissions for "others" for their personal files, and rails continues to work normally, until it stops working unexpectedly when it's time to run the container.

### Steps to reproduce

```
mkdir example
docker run -it --rm -u 1000:1000 -v ./example:/app ruby bash
cd /app
gem install rails
rails new foobar
exit
cd example/foobar
sudo chmod -R o= .
docker build --no-cache -t example . && docker run -it --rm -u 1000:1000 -e RAILS_ENV=development example
```
Notice the error:
```
/bin/bash: /rails/bin/docker-entrypoint: Permission denied
```
### Expected behavior

Expected to be able to execute `docker-entrypoint`.

### Actual behavior

Image finishes building successfully, but container fails to start because we don't have permissions to run `docker-entrypoint`.



### System configuration

**Rails version**:  8.0.2

**Ruby version**: 3.4.5

title: `NoMethodError`: undefined method 'dimensions=' for an instance of `PG::TextEncoder::Array`
need_summary: The developer wanted to know if the pg gem version mismatch causing a NoMethodError during cache deserialization poses a security risk and how to address it, and the answer points to the pg source change that added the `dimensions` attribute (GitHub code link) as the concrete cause.
security_topic: cache serialization incompatibility across pg gem versions
question_text: I'm not sure if this is a Rails issue or a pg gem issue, but I'm reporting it to warn if someone is going to upgrade pg gem.
answer_text:
Here's the pg code that is problematic: https://github.com/ged/ruby-pg/blob/b77e86c478c294fd74ed187b7573df2665903209/lib/pg/coder.rb#L17-L23

Basically like this:
```rb
hash.each do |key, val|
  send("#{key}=", val)
end
```
So if new attributes are added, there's a good chance of this happening again. Probably it should not make such assumptions.

For the rails side of things, I'm unsure if it would be a good idea to swallow arbitrary errors as cache misses. It would help this case for sure though and `ArgumentError` is already rescued to handle missing constants.
thread_text:
ISSUE #55423: `NoMethodError`: undefined method 'dimensions=' for an instance of `PG::TextEncoder::Array`
Author: moofkit
Date: 2025-07-30T14:05:47Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
Cached data serialized with pg gem 1.6.0 cannot be deserialized with pg gem 1.5.9, causing:
```
NoMethodError: undefined method 'dimensions=' for an instance of PG::TextEncoder::Array
```

This occurs during rolling deployments when:
1. New instances deploy with pg gem 1.6.0 and cache ActiveRecord objects containing PostgreSQL arrays
2. Old instances still running pg gem 1.5.9 try to read the same cached data
3. Shared cache (Redis/Memcached) contains mixed data from both versions
4. Production traffic randomly hits either version, causing intermittent failures

### Steps to reproduce

Save as `pg_cache_bug_reproduction.rb`:

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails"
  gem "pg", ENV.fetch("PG_VERSION")
end

require "active_record/railtie"
require "minitest/autorun"

ENV["DATABASE_URL"] ||= "postgresql:test"

class TestApp < Rails::Application
  config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f
  config.eager_load = false
  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"
  config.cache_store = :file_store, "tmp/cache"
end

Rails.application.initialize!

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :users, force: true do |t|
    t.string :tags, array: true
  end
end

class User < ActiveRecord::Base
end

class PGCacheSerializationBugTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  def setup
    @user = User.create!(tags: ["test", "example"])
    Rails.cache.clear if PG::VERSION == "1.6.0"
  end

  def test_cache_compatibility_across_pg_versions
    if PG::VERSION == "1.6.0"
      Rails.cache.write("test_key", @user)
      user = Rails.cache.read("test_key")
      assert_equal @user.tags, user.tags
    elsif PG::VERSION == "1.5.9"
      user = Rails.cache.read("test_key") # This raises the error
      assert_equal @user.tags, user.tags
    end
  end
end
```

```bash
PG_VERSION='1.6.0' ruby pg_cache_bug_reproduction.rb

PG_VERSION='1.5.9' ruby pg_cache_bug_reproduction.rb
```

## Expected behavior

Cached ActiveRecord objects with PostgreSQL array attributes should be readable across compatible pg gem versions during canary deployments, or Rails should handle the deserialization gracefully when versions are mixed.

I'm not sure if this is a Rails issue or a pg gem issue, but I'm reporting it to warn if someone is going to upgrade pg gem.

## Actual behavior

```
NoMethodError: undefined method 'dimensions=' for an instance of PG::TextEncoder::Array
    /gems/pg-1.5.9/lib/pg/coder.rb:21:in 'block in PG::Coder#initialize'
    /gems/pg-1.5.9/lib/pg/coder.rb:20:in 'Hash#each'
    /gems/pg-1.5.9/lib/pg/coder.rb:20:in 'PG::Coder#initialize'
    /gems/pg-1.5.9/lib/pg/coder.rb:48:in 'PG::Coder#marshal_load'
    <internal:marshal>:34:in 'Marshal.load'
    /gems/activesupport-8.0.2/lib/active_support/cache/serializer_with_fallback.rb:40:in 'marshal_load'
```

Root cause
- [pg 1.6.0 introduces a `dimensions` attribute](https://github.com/ged/ruby-pg/pull/622) in `PG::TextEncoder::Array` during marshal serialization
- pg 1.5.9 doesn't recognize this attribute during `marshal_load`, causing the error

## System configuration

**Rails version:** 8.0.2

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @Earlopain 2025-07-31T08:32:33Z:
Here's the pg code that is problematic: https://github.com/ged/ruby-pg/blob/b77e86c478c294fd74ed187b7573df2665903209/lib/pg/coder.rb#L17-L23

Basically like this:
```rb
hash.each do |key, val|
  send("#{key}=", val)
end
```
So if new attributes are added, there's a good chance of this happening again. Probably it should not make such assumptions.

For the rails side of things, I'm unsure if it would be a good idea to swallow arbitrary errors as cache misses. It would help this case for sure though and `ArgumentError` is already rescued to handle missing constants.

There's also this snippet from the guides [Avoid Caching Instances of Active Record Objects](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/caching_with_rails.html#avoid-caching-instances-of-active-record-objects) 😉 
---
[c2] @moofkit 2025-07-31T08:39:46Z:
> There's also this snippet from the guides [Avoid Caching Instances of Active Record Objects](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/caching_with_rails.html#avoid-caching-instances-of-active-record-objects) 😉

Highly agree! That's one more reason to avoid such a usage of caching. But I see it pretty often unfortunately.

---

title: ActiveRecord does not escape NUL bytes for SQLite3
need_summary: The developer wanted to know if ActiveRecord would raise a clear error for strings containing NUL bytes when using SQLite3, and the maintainer referenced PR #55375 which adds an ArgumentError check for such cases.
security_topic: exception handling for NUL byte strings in SQLite adapter
question_text: Either there should be a sensible exception thrown that tells you that it can't do the SQL statement because of a string containing a NUL byte (analogous to what happens if you try to insert bad utf8), or it should somehow manage to insert a string with a NUL byte in it without truncating it (unsure if that is possible with SQLite).
answer_text: I’ve opened a PR to address it: #55375. The PR adds a check in the SQLite adapter that raises a clear ArgumentError when a string containing a null byte (\x00) is passed. This avoids the confusing SQLite3::SQLException: unrecognized token error and aligns with how Rails handles invalid string inputs in other cases like bad UTF-8.
thread_text:
ISSUE #55373: ActiveRecord does not escape NUL bytes for SQLite3
Author: jes
Date: 2025-07-20T21:10:23Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
### Steps to reproduce

1. Try to insert something that contains a NUL byte in a string field, in a SQLite3 database
2. It fails with an "unrecognised token" error instead of either working or failing with an appropriate error

Example here: https://asciinema.org/a/QFuSdpD8LWlGLfnsVSgJtu5fD

Example steps are:

```
rails new jestest
cd jestest
rails generate model TestModel foo:string
rails db:migrate
rails console
TestModel.create!(foo:"jes\0test")
```

I tried to reopen #947 but I don't have permission so I've created a new ticket.

### Expected behavior

Either there should be a sensible exception thrown that tells you that it can't do the SQL statement because of a string containing a NUL byte (analogous to what happens if you try to insert bad utf8), or it should somehow manage to insert a string with a NUL byte in it without truncating it (unsure if that is possible with SQLite).

### Actual behavior

The program crashes with an error about an unrecognised token in the generated SQL statement.

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.0.2

**Ruby version**: 3.4.5


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @himanshukale36 2025-07-21T03:46:38Z:
Hi @jes 👋
I’ve opened a PR to address it: [#55375](https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/55375).

The PR adds a check in the SQLite adapter that raises a clear ArgumentError when a string containing a null byte (\x00) is passed. This avoids the confusing SQLite3::SQLException: unrecognized token error and aligns with how Rails handles invalid string inputs in other cases like bad UTF-8.

Let me know if you have any feedback!

Closing as wontfix. See discussion in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/55375.

TL;DR; It's indeed an annoying behavior but having to check all strings for NULL bytes is costly for something that's very rare.

thread_text: ISSUE #55245: Handle links and other safe content inside translations Author: runephilosof-abtion Date: 2025-06-26T06:50:35Z Labels: stale State: closed [c0] Currently, if I want to put a link into a translation, I have to do ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)).html_safe %> ``` or ```erb <%= t(".text_html", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` However, the `text_html` translation should not have to know whether the `insert` contains html or not. ~Also, the `insert` translation cannot have unescaped html content, because it is used as content inside another `_html` translation.~ The rails i18n guide does not mention how to do this nicely. The best would be if rails-i18n could handle it automatically by being aware of SafeBuffer. ```yml text: some <> text with an %{insert} text_html: some <> text with an %{insert} insert: a link, properly escaping <> ``` ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` Rails-i18n should handle safe joining the above example. `link_to` returns a `html_safe` string, so this should output ```html some <> text with an a link, properly escaping <> ``` --- COMMENTS --- [c1] @runephilosof-abtion 2025-06-26T06:51:42Z: Related issue in https://github.com/svenfuchs/rails-i18n/issues/1147, which was closed with a suggestion of implementing it in Rails. --- [c2] @dari-us 2025-06-27T19:31:21Z: I'm not sure I understand the use case for this. What prevents you from putting the `` directly into the translation YAML file? ``` text_html: 'Some >< text with a link, properly escaping ><' ``` Yes, you have to escape the content of the `` yourself in this case, but isn't it static anyway? If you really need this grade of freedom for the `insert`, the second option seems totally fine to me. Maybe the contents of `.insert` is conditional. 1. A translation should not need to know whether its variables contain html. 2. You might consider translations to be untrusted user input, except `_html` ones, which would be more expensive to maintain. 3. Rails already has the concept of SafeBuffer, so why throw that information away when translating. --- [c4] @runephilosof-abtion 2025-07-03T09:05:33Z: It would need to be changed in https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/36601bbb02bc3570f5609db2127c77afca575d6c/activesupport/lib/active_support/html_safe_translation.rb and https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/actionpack/lib/abstract_controller/translation.rb#L28. # Authentication generator missing rate limiting on PasswordsController

## Description

The Rails 8 authentication generator is missing rate limiting on the `PasswordsController` despite ActionMailer being available. This leaves the password reset endpoint vulnerable to abuse.

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Create a new Rails application
rails new test_app
cd test_app

# Verify ActionMailer is available
rails runner "puts defined?(ActionMailer::Railtie)"
# Output: "constant"

# Generate authentication
rails generate authentication

# Check the generated PasswordsController
cat app/controllers/passwords_controller.rb
```

## Expected behavior

The generated `PasswordsController` should include rate limiting on the `create` action when ActionMailer is available:

```ruby
rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create, with: -> { redirect_to new_password_path, alert: "Try again later." }
```

This protection is essential to prevent abuse of the password reset email functionality.

## Actual behavior

The generated `PasswordsController` is missing the rate limiting line, despite ActionMailer being available. The controller includes the `create` action that sends password reset emails, but lacks the rate limiting protection that should be conditionally included when `ActionMailer::Railtie` is defined.

This leaves the password reset endpoint vulnerable to abuse for email spam attacks.

## System configuration
- **Rails version**: 8.0.0
- **Ruby version**: 3.2.0

## Additional context

The authentication generator template appears to have an ERB conditional that should include rate limiting when ActionMailer is available:

```erb
<%- if defined?(ActionMailer::Railtie) -%>
rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create, with: -> { redirect_to new_password_path, alert: "Try again later." }
<%- end -%>
```

However, this conditional is not evaluating correctly during template generation, resulting in missing rate limiting protection.

title: ActiveRecord call `.lease_connection` inside `.transaction` cause connection leak
need_summary: The developer needed to know how to prevent the ActiveRecord connection leak (a potential availability/security risk) when using lease_connection inside a transaction, and the answer cites the Rails API docs and PR #51192, recommending calling release_connection or using with_connection(prevent_permanent_checkout: true).
security_topic: connection leak causing resource exhaustion in ActiveRecord transactions
question_text:
So how i can easily receive connection without this behaviour in complicated, nested code? For example:
```ruby
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  do_call
end

def do_call
  # ActiveRecord::Base.connection or something else that will release connection after #transaction block
end
```
answer_text:
# call `release_connection` when you're done with a connection
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  do_call
end
ActiveRecore::Base.release_connection

# or only checkout connections where you need them (nesting with_connection always gives you the same connection)
def do_call
  Base.with_connection do |c|
  end
end
thread_text:
ISSUE #55185: ActiveRecord call `.lease_connection` inside `.transaction` cause connection leak
Author: tevvi
Date: 2025-06-11T14:24:26Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
### Steps to reproduce
1. rails c
2. run code:
```ruby
puts "Before: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  ActiveRecord::Base.lease_connection
end
puts "After: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
```
### Expected behavior
```
Before:
After: 
```

### Actual behavior
```
Before:
After: #<ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::Mysql2Adapter>
```

#### Explanation
When .lease_connection called in .transaction, connection is not released when exiting from .with_connection. So connection is leaked(or stuck) to current thread

#### Why it is a problem
Our application send mixed db queries with http requests, which much slower than db queries so. And we faced with connection limit on mysql server side. So we have to release(return back to process pool) all obtained db connections before start execute http requests

#### When we faced with it
1. Our legacy have dirty call db queries(.connection.execute) inside transaction, but nested in several methods. So refactor(to forward connection from .transaction yield) is complicated
2. When we added after_commit_everywhere 1.6.0 to application(rails 7.2.2.1 only) to use Sidekiq.transactional_push!. And following code cause connection leak:
```ruby
class MyWorker
  include Sidekiq::Worker
  sidekiq_options queue: :default

  def perform; end
end

puts "Before: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  MyWorker.perform_async
end
puts "After: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
```

Connection leak because next trace:
https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/blob/v6.5.12/lib/sidekiq/transaction_aware_client.rb#L16
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L100
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L111
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L144
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L172

### System configuration
rails 7.2.2.1 with ruby 3.3.2
rails 8.0.2 with ruby 3.4.4


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @skipkayhil 2025-06-11T14:35:46Z:
Isn't this by design? The API docs say

> The connection will remain leased for the entire duration of the request or job, or until [release_connection](https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/ConnectionHandling.html#method-i-release_connection) is called.

So if you want the connection returned to the pool you must use `release_connection` after `lease_connection`
---
[c2] @tevvi 2025-06-11T14:49:13Z:
@skipkayhil So how i can easily receive connection without this behaviour in complicated, nested code? 
For example:
```ruby
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  do_call
end

def do_call
  # ActiveRecord::Base.connection or something else that will release connection after #transaction block
end
```
---
[c3] @skipkayhil 2025-06-11T14:57:18Z:
```ruby
# call `release_connection` when you're done with a connection
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  do_call
end
ActiveRecore::Base.release_connection

# or only checkout connections where you need them (nesting with_connection always gives you the same connection)
def do_call
  Base.with_connection do |c|
  end
end
```
---
[c4] @tevvi 2025-06-11T15:13:13Z:
@skipkayhil So next step to rewrite all code(application and gems) which use ActiveRecore::Base.lease_connection. I think it is a complicated solution

Easier solution is return back previous logic. Add method sticky_connection with new behaviour(The connection will remain leased for the entire duration of the request or job, or until release_connection is called.) and rewrite lease_connection to release connection after with_connection block
---
[c5] @skipkayhil 2025-06-11T15:15:02Z:
> Add method sticky_connection with new behaviour(The connection will remain leased for the entire duration of the request or job, or until release_connection is called.)

This is how `ActiveRecord::Base.connection` has always worked (1 connection per request/job). `with_connection`/`release_connection` _is_ the new behavior that allows you to not have a single connection checked out for a whole request/job.
---
[c6] @byroot 2025-06-12T06:45:00Z:
What @skipkayhil said, this was done by design to not break code that had expectations about the connection being sticky: https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/51192

You can manually call `release_connection` after, or wrap the whole thing in `.with_connection(prevent_permanent_checkout: true)`.
---

title: Segmentation fault on ActionController::Live
need_summary: The developer asked how to capture a C backtrace of the Ruby segfault while the process is running, and the answer provided concrete steps to enable core dumps and use gdb (see https://mvidner.blogspot.com/2019/01/backtrace-from-core-dump-with-gdb.html)
security_topic: capturing native C backtrace for Ruby segmentation fault
question_text: How do I capture the C backtrace of the crash given that the process will still be alive and other code paths will be continuously executed.
answer_text:
Ideally you configure your server so that it stores core dumps. From there you can use `gdb` or `lldb` to open the core dump with the `ruby` binary and get a backtrace out of it.

I quickly googled to see if there was some sort of guide , and found a few:

  - https://mvidner.blogspot.com/2019/01/backtrace-from-core-dump-with-gdb.html
  - https://www.aha.io/engineering/articles/debugging-ruby-the-hard-way

Hope this helps.

Apologies in advance for not strictly following the issue template.

This issue has been happening on our production and I haven't been able to reproduce it locally. However, I am fairly confidently that the problem was introduced in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/52731. Reverting to the previous behavior where a new thread is initialized for each request resolves the problem.

The only instance we use `ActionController::Live` is through `ActiveStorage::Blobs::ProxyController`, so, there's no custom controller code is involved.

- Some of our clients have very unireliable internet connection, which means that avoiding redirection and serving the blobs from the same host provides slightly better UX. These streaming connections can also be exhausting and very slow

My best guess is that a use-after-free problem is happening after: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/0ac3fba6ee5f7d1680024a4925eee6069095487b/actionpack/lib/action_controller/metal/live.rb#L304-L305 (but what do I know 🤷)

**Ruby version**: 3.4.4

comments.author: byroot
comments.body:
Almost by definition, a SEGFAULT cannot be a Rails bug. This is either a Ruby bug or a bug in one C extension.

Not to say we shouldn't investigate this, but the resolution won't be on the Rails side (at best we can do some workaround).

Unfortunately, the crash reports you shared don't include the C backtrace, so it's not easy to tell what's happening here. All I can say is since the two Ruby backtraces are in random places, I suspect this is crashing during GC, hence this is likely to be a memory corruption issue. (which makes it even harder to debug without a repro).

comments.body:
> How do I capture the C backtrace of the crash given that the process will still be alive and other code paths will be continuously executed.

Ideally you configure your server so that it stores core dumps. From there you can use `gdb` or `lldb` to open the core dump with the `ruby` binary and get a backtrace out of it.

I quickly googled to see if there was some sort of guide , and found a few:

  - https://mvidner.blogspot.com/2019/01/backtrace-from-core-dump-with-gdb.html
  - https://www.aha.io/engineering/articles/debugging-ruby-the-hard-way


Hope this helps.

comments.author: byroot
comments.body:
> * ruby:alpine based Docker image

Hum, I wonder if you aren't simply running out of stack space. `alpine` is infamous for having extremely small stack space for secondary threads and lots of programs just straight out crash on alpine.

Most systems give `8MiB` of stack to all threads, but Alpine (well `musl`) only give `128KiB` to secondary threads).

So it would be worth trying to increase the stack size before digging into core dumps and gdb: https://serverfault.com/questions/1123052/alpine-linux-on-docker-is-it-possible-to-configure-the-thread-stack-size

It was on my list to remove threading from `Live` altogether (there is no need for it whatsoever) but other things took priority.

Kind of, the crux of the problem is that the spec says thread local state (including current attributes etc) must be copied: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/4256e620570bf1dc86a597618065ec18a1efa9df/actionpack/test/controller/live_stream_test.rb#L528-L571

This is so that whatever state your middleware may have set is still accessible.

The problem is it's impossible for generic code like AC::Live to know what in there should be:

  - Shared.
  - Copied.
  - Deep Copied.
  - Or simply not passed over.

I'm still unable to repro the reported crash, but I suspect something end up being shared between two threads while it shouldn't. If it was identified we could do an ad hoc fix for this particular issue, but the more general design issue would remain.

### Steps to reproduce

Can't reproduce it using the generic bug template, only by running `rails test` in a rails project. I'm probably holding it wrong by using the `it` block var in a different block scope, but it shouldn't segfault.

```ruby
class SegfaultTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test "segfaults" do
    [1].each do
      begin
        puts it
      rescue => e
        puts it
      end
    end
  end
end
```
Rails 7.2.2 repo with the segfaulting test case here: https://github.com/scarhand/rails-test-segfault

### Expected behavior

It should raise an error that assertions are missing, but it should not segfault.

title: `Rails.error.subscribe` not reporting `rescue_responses` when `enable_reloading = false`
need_summary: The developer asked whether Rails can be configured to report rescued responses (e.g., 404 errors) in production, and the maintainer pointed to PR #55055 which adds a config option to enable this reporting.
security_topic: error reporting of rescued responses in production
question_text: I tried to find a setting that enables reporting them in production as well, but haven't found anything.
answer_text: I created a pull request that adds said config option to report `rescue_responses` in production. It does **not** fix the weird interaction with `config.enable_reloading`, because I was unable to figure out how to fix it. On a side note, errors are never reported if `config.consider_all_requests_local = true` and the `ActionDispatch::DebugExceptions` is used to render the response, not sure whether it is intended. However, I think using the error reporter only makes sense in `production`, so I am not that motivated to fix weird interactions with development/test-only config option values. https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/55055
thread_text:
ISSUE #55040: `Rails.error.subscribe` not reporting `rescue_responses` when `enable_reloading = false`
Author: dari-us
Date: 2025-05-09T21:22:08Z
Labels: attached PR
State: open

[c0]
### Steps to reproduce

In a fresh Rails 8.0.2 app, add to `config/application.rb`:

```
Rails.error.subscribe(Class.new do
  def self.report(e, **)
    File.open("errors.log", "a+") { it.write(Rails.env.to_s + " " + Time.current.to_s + " " + e.class.name) }
  end
end)
```
Also, in `config/environments/development.rb`, set `consider_all_requests_local` to `false`.

Then, generate a route and a Controller action, where you manually `raise` any rescued response, f.e. `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`.


Running the server in `development`, the error gets written to the file, as expected.
However, running the server in `production`, nothing gets written.

I tried to find a setting that enables reporting them in `production` as well, but haven't found anything.


Also, `ActionController::RoutingError`  is never reported regardless of environment.


Compared to using a middleware, using `Rails.error.subscribe` seems inferior to me (at least for Controllers), since it has a lot of "blind spots", especially in `production`. Or am I missing something?


### Expected behavior

The error is reported regardless of `Rails.env`. Also, `ActionController::RoutingError` should be reported.

### Actual behavior

Errors in `ActionDispatch::ExceptionWrapper.rescue_responses` are not reported in `production` and `ActionController::RoutingError` is not reported at all.

### System configuration

**Rails version**:  8.0.2

**Ruby version**: 3.4.3


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @maxfelsher 2025-05-11T17:17:21Z:
I can confirm that the behavior for rescued responses differs between the default development configuration and the default production configuration. Specifically, it seems to be related to `enable_reloading`, though I'm not sure why. Reproducible test case below; it fails (the subscriber is not called) with `config.enable_reloading` set to false (as in production) and passes (the subscriber is called) when it's set to true (as in development).

I suspect that the production behavior may be what was intended, since 404s, 400s, and the like are the expected response when a client submits an incorrect request, and you don't necessarily want your error reporting service to be clogged up with these "errors" because some botnet or scanning tool sent a bunch of random requests. On the other hand, sometimes those incorrect requests are caused by your application's own code, so it'd be nice to be have some visibility on them. Someone from the core team will probably have to weigh in.

I took a quick look at the `ActionController::RoutingError` issue you mentioned (that it wasn't reported in either development or production). I don't know exactly how you were raising it, but I did notice that `raise ActionController::RoutingError` behaved differently in the test case below. However, the issue there was that it looks like that error class requires a message to be set, so I was actually hitting an ArgumentError when trying to raise the routing error. When I changed it to `raise ActionController::RoutingError.new('anything')`, it behaved the same as the test case below. I'm not sure if that's the issue you were facing, as that should have still caused entries to be added to your `errors.log`, just as ArgumentErrors instead of ActionController::RoutingErrors.

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails"
  # If you want to test against edge Rails replace the previous line with this:
  # gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"
end

require "action_controller/railtie"
require "minitest/autorun"
require "rack/test"

class TestApp < Rails::Application
  config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f
  config.root = __dir__
  config.eager_load = false
  config.hosts << "example.org"
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"

  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)

  config.enable_reloading = false # Change this to true to cause test to pass

  Rails.error.subscribe(Class.new do
    def self.report(...)
      $subscriber_called = true
    end
  end)
end
Rails.application.initialize!

Rails.application.routes.draw do
  get "/", to: "test#index"
end

class TestController < ActionController::Base
  include Rails.application.routes.url_helpers

  def index
    raise AbstractController::ActionNotFound
  end
end

$subscriber_called = false

class BugTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  include Rack::Test::Methods

  def test_subscriber_called
    get "/"
    assert $subscriber_called # Passes if enable_reloading set to true, fails if set to false
  end

  private
    def app
      Rails.application
    end
end
```
---
[c2] @dari-us 2025-05-12T07:50:27Z:
Thanks a lot for providing a test case and more insight into the cause of this issue.
I see both points as valid, as for me, I want to catch those `rescue_responses` as well, because they may be caused by my own app code and it's abysmal UX to have a blind spot there.
The specific `ActionController::RoutingError` I meant is the one thrown by the router in case the route cannot be found. Call `get "/bleargh"` in your test case to see what I mean, it never calls the subscriber, regardless of `enable_reloading`.
Maybe the best way to solve this for both worlds is providing a config option, like `Rails.application.config.action_dispatch.report_rescued_responses = true/false`.

On another note, the subscriber should also be called inside the rails runner and jobs (according to the docs), but not sure how to test it and not sure whether `rescue_responses` are honored there as well.
In case they are honored there as well, maybe the config option better fits in the `active_support` namespace.
---
[c3] @dari-us 2025-05-12T08:34:06Z:
I can confirm, that for jobs, **every** error is reported, even the ones included in `rescue_responses`.
Which makes sense, since `rescue_responses` map exceptions to response codes, which does not apply to jobs.

```ruby

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails", "8.0.2"
  # If you want to test against edge Rails replace the previous line with this:

  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_job/railtie"

  config.enable_reloading = false
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"
  config.active_job.queue_adapter = :test

  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)

  Rails.error.subscribe(Class.new do
    def self.report(...)
      $subscriber_called = true
    end
  end)
end
Rails.application.initialize!

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :models, force: true
end

$subscriber_called = false

class Model < ActiveRecord::Base; end

class BuggyJob < ActiveJob::Base
  def perform
    Model.find(1)
  end
end

class BuggyJobTest < ActiveJob::TestCase
  def test_stuff
    perform_enqueued_jobs do
      BuggyJob.perform_later
    rescue
      # noop
    end
    assert $subscriber_called
  end
```

---
[c4] @dari-us 2025-05-12T21:50:04Z:
I created a pull request that adds said config option to report `rescue_responses` in production.
It does **not** fix the weird interaction with `config.enable_reloading`, because I was unable to figure out how to fix it.
On a side note, errors are never reported if `config.consider_all_requests_local = true` and the `ActionDispatch::DebugExceptions` is used to render the response, not sure whether it is intended.

However, I think using the error reporter only makes sense in `production`, so I am not that motivated to fix weird interactions with development/test-only config option values.

https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/55055
---
[c5] @maxfelsher 2025-05-14T03:34:32Z:
@byroot Thanks for clarifying that errors in `rescue_responses` aren't intended to be reported by the error reporter! There's still the odd behavior that if `enable_reloading` is true, those errors *do* get reported. Is that intentional? It seems like it could lead to confusing differences between development and production like the one that caused this issue to be opened.

With a little more digging, I determined that setting `enable_reloading` to true but then removing the `ActionDispatch::Reloader` middleware stopped the errors from being reported, so it seems like it's something about that middleware that's causing the `rescue_responses` errors to be reported. And looking at the code, that makes some sense: `ActionDispatch::ShowExceptions` is in the default middleware stack between the standard `ActionDispatch::Executor` and the reloader, so ShowExceptions can only affect the following code when it's being run in the context of the standard executor and not in the context of the reloader:

https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/a3b37ff166a925f7e069c9068f7ee92808da6e82/actionpack/lib/action_dispatch/middleware/executor.rb#L15-L29
---
[c6] @byroot 2025-05-14T06:52:07Z:
Yes, the reloader is an executor, hence it reports errors it catch. And since it's lower in the middleware stack that cause a difference compared to production.

Would be nice to fix indeed, even though I don't think it's a huge deal.

title: Signed cookies use SHA-1 by default
need_summary: The developer asked if the default signed cookie digest using SHA-1 is a security concern and whether it will be changed, and the maintainer responded with a concrete PR (https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/55017) that addresses the issue.
security_topic: default signing algorithm for Rails signed cookies
question_text: Signed cookies use a secure-by-default signing method such as SHA-256.
answer_text: I have raised a PR to address this, please see: https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/55017.
thread_text:
ISSUE #54926: Signed cookies use SHA-1 by default
Author: elondres-mim
Date: 2025-04-15T17:49:03Z
Labels: attached PR
State: open

[c0]
### Steps to reproduce

<!-- (Guidelines for creating a bug report are [available
here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#creating-a-bug-report)) -->

In a new rails app, create a signed cookie with `cookies.signed[:foo] = 'bar'`.

### Expected behavior

Signed cookies use a secure-by-default signing method such as SHA-256.

<!-- Tell us what should happen -->

### Actual behavior

In the controller if you then call `cookies.send :signed_cookie_digest`, you get "SHA1".


https://guides.rubyonrails.org/configuring.html#config-action-dispatch-signed-cookie-digest does document that the default for signed_cookie_digest is "SHA1", though the upgrade guide for Rails 7.0 implied this was changing to SHA-256:
https://guides.rubyonrails.org/upgrading_ruby_on_rails.html#digest-class-for-activesupport-digest-changing-to-sha256

and the active support digest class did in fact change to SHA-256:
https://guides.rubyonrails.org/configuring.html#config-active-support-hash-digest-class

but not the cookie digest class it seems.
<!-- Tell us what happens instead -->

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.0.1

**Ruby version**:  3.3.5, I suspect any version would work.

title: ActionDispatch::Cookies::CookieOverflow not raised on cookie overflow
need_summary: The developer wanted to know if Rails' CookieOverflow check includes the cookie name, and the answer cites the check_for_overflow! method in the Rails code showing it only validates the value size
security_topic: Rails cookie overflow detection mismatch with browser limits
question_text: ActionDispatch::Cookies::CookieOverflow not raised on cookie overflow
answer_text:
The check indeed only consider the cookie value, and ignore the name.

```ruby
        def check_for_overflow!(name, options)
          if options[:value].bytesize > MAX_COOKIE_SIZE
            raise CookieOverflow, "#{name} cookie overflowed with size #{options[:value].bytesize} bytes"
          end
        end
```
thread_text: ISSUE #54838: ActionDispatch::Cookies::CookieOverflow not raised on cookie overflow Author: perryn Date: 2025-03-30T12:39:40Z Labels: actionpack, attached PR State: closed [c0] It is possible to generate a session cookie that is silently dropped by the browser because it is too large, but which does not trigger rails's overflow check. I suspect that this is because rails performs the check on the length of the value of the cookie only, but browsers check the sum of the length of the cookie's name, value, and attributes ( as per [section 6.1 of rfc6265](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6265#section-6.1) ) ### Steps to reproduce Put something like this in a rails app ``` def reproduce reset_session session[:a] = "a" * 2000 # you will need to adjust this number end after_action :reproduce ``` Increase the number until a request to the app generates a ActionDispatch::Cookies::CookieOverflow Now slightly decrease the number again until no ActionDispatch::Cookies::CookieOverflow is raised ### Expected behavior Since the overflow check has passed the browser should accept the latest session cookie ### Actual behavior The browser will reject the cookie as too large. Any changes made to the session in the last request will have been lost. In Chrome for example you can check whether the cookie was rejected by opening dev tools, going to the network tab and checking the Set-Cookie response header for a warning icon: ### System configuration **Rails version**: 7.1.3.4 **Ruby version**: 3.3.0 --- COMMENTS --- [c1] @perryn 2025-03-30T12:44:53Z: I discovered this after experiencing a production problem where session changes were disappearing. The culprit turned out to be a large JWT from a third-party security vendor in the session, but the fact that I was not seeing CookieOverflow errors mislead me for some time. --- [c2] @byroot 2025-03-31T08:16:30Z: The check indeed only consider the cookie value, and ignore the name. ```ruby def check_for_overflow!(name, options) if options[:value].bytesize > MAX_COOKIE_SIZE raise CookieOverflow, "#{name} cookie overflowed with size #{options[:value].bytesize} bytes" end end ``` ---

thread_text:
ISSUE #54819: Destroying non-existing record succeeds, triggering after_destroy callbacks
Author: Linuus
Date: 2025-03-26T09:14:13Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
### Steps to reproduce

Run the script below, `after_destroy` is triggered twice as can be seen in the output.

```ruby
require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails"
  # If you want to test against edge Rails replace the previous line with this:
  # gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"

  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record/railtie"
require "minitest/autorun"

# This connection will do for database-independent bug reports.
ENV["DATABASE_URL"] = "sqlite3::memory:"

class TestApp < Rails::Application
  config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f
  config.eager_load = false
  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"

  config.active_record.encryption.primary_key = "primary_key"
  config.active_record.encryption.deterministic_key = "deterministic_key"
  config.active_record.encryption.key_derivation_salt = "key_derivation_salt"
end
Rails.application.initialize!

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :posts, force: true do |t|
  end
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  after_destroy(:hello)

  def hello
    puts "AFTER DESTROY TIGGERED"
  end
end

class BugTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  def test_association_stuff
    post = Post.create!
    post_copy = Post.first

    post.destroy!
    post_copy.destroy! # Shouldn't this fail?
  end
end

```

### Expected behavior

The second `destroy!` should fail and not trigger the `after_destroy` callback.

I'm not sure if this is intended or not but what happens now if there are multiple requests coming in to destroy a record, only one will destroy it but all requests will trigger the `after_destroy` callbacks.

Is this intended? If it is, is there any way to avoid this issue? Say you are updating something in an `after_destroy` callback when the record is destroyed.

### Actual behavior

The call to `destroy!` succeeds and triggers the `after_destroy` callback.

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 7-8

**Ruby version**: 3.3.5


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @eileencodes 2025-03-26T13:09:21Z:
Hi! This is intentional behavior, persistence isn't required for `after_destroy` callbacks to run. More details in https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/48841
---
[c2] @Linuus 2025-03-26T13:42:54Z:
> Hi! This is intentional behavior, persistence isn't required for `after_destroy` callbacks to run. More details in [#48841](https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/48841)

Thank you for the reply.

But isn't that issue a bit different? There it's about a record that was never persisted? In this case the DELETE statement is sent, but it doesn't delete anything.

Wouldn't it make sense for the `destroy(!)` to check if any row was affected? It's similar to updating a "stale" object, no?
---
[c3] @eileencodes 2025-03-26T15:24:39Z:
I see what you're saying but I still think this is intended behavior. The update method doesn't check whether there were previous changes that are unsaved, and the delete method doesn't check if it was previously deleted. Until it's reloaded `post_copy` exists in memory. There's also the downside of having to emit an extra query every time you want to delete something.

Can you explain why this behavior is problematic for your app? It's not like it's deleting records it shouldn't. And if you don't want the second destroy to succeed, the record could be reloaded before destroy (which will fire a not found error).
---
[c4] @Linuus 2025-03-26T16:50:57Z:
Well a reload minimizes the likelihood of the race condition but it doesn’t eliminate it.

The issue we see is that we update something in the after_destroy callback. Then, say we get 10 concurrent requests to delete a record. Worst case is that 1 request actually deletes the record but all 10 fires the after_destroy callback.

And would we really need to fire another query? It looks like the DELETE is always happening just that only one actually deletes. Doesn’t that return the number of deleted rows already? So we could just check if the query actually deleted anything?
---
[c5] @ozone4real 2025-03-26T17:31:52Z:
To add to @Linuus' comment, there also doesn't seem to be a way to check in the after_destroy callback if a database DELETE actually happened. If there is one let us know. I tried these:

- #reload: This always raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` in the after_destroy callback when you call #destroy! on both the persisted record (post) and deleted copy (post_copy). This is because for the persisted record, the database DELETE has already happened by the time the callback runs. So `#reload` can't be used to to make a decision on whether to trigger the side-effect.
- #destroyed?: This returns `true` in the callback for both.
- #persisted? returns `false` for both.

Using the example in the description:

```ruby
class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  after_destroy(:hello)

  def hello
     puts destroyed?
     puts persisted?
     reload
  rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound
    puts "Record not found"
  end
end


post = Post.create!
post_copy = Post.first

post.destroy! # prints true, false, Record not found
post_copy.destroy! # prints true, false, Record not found
```
---

ISSUE #54785: ActiveRecord Encryption `compress: false` and `compressor:` break encryption contexts
Author: fletchto99
